sections.overview: The Great Crested Grebe is a large waterbird of wetlands across Europe, Asia, parts of Africa, Australia and New Zealand. It dives for prey, nests on floating vegetation and raises its young on water. Northern birds often move to ice-free wintering waters. Breeding populations also occur eastward to Mongolia, with winter visitors reaching southern Asia.
sections.identification: Adults are about 45–51 cm long, with similar plumage in both sexes. Breeding birds show a black double crest and chestnut-and-black facial ruff; in winter these ornaments shrink. Striped heads distinguish juveniles. Their long neck, pointed reddish bill, short tail and pale underside complete a distinctive profile on the water. British adults average about 993 g; the species is about 45–51 cm long, with similar adult plumage in both sexes.
sections.habitat: Breeding grebes favour freshwater lakes and reservoirs, often with reed-fringed sheltered margins. Calm shallows provide plants and anchorage for floating nests. In winter, some move to larger lakes, estuaries or coasts, depending on ice and food. They also use brackish lagoons and bays, provided shallow water and vegetation offer secure nesting cover.
sections.diet: Fish are its main prey, swallowed head-first after underwater pursuit; aquatic insects, crustaceans and amphibians also feature. The separate toe lobes act like paddles and rudders beneath the surface. Grebes swallow loose feathers while preening; stomach studies found feathers mixed with indigestible fish remains in regurgitated pellets. Their precise digestive role remains debated. At one Dutch lake, grebes fed at dawn and dusk when smelt rose nearer the surface, shortening dives; this pattern is local, not universal.
sections.behavior: Pairs defend nesting territories. In their well-known display, both birds raise their crests, shake their heads, dive and rise together while offering water plants. This synchronized weed ceremony helps maintain the pair bond. Their legs are set far back for efficient swimming and diving, but make walking on land awkward. Females also advertise during pair formation with a loud metallic note followed by a softer purring sound.
sections.reproduction: The pair builds a floating platform of water plants among reeds. Usually three or four eggs hatch after both adults share 27–29 days of incubation. Chicks leave the nest soon after hatching; able to swim, they still depend on both parents for warmth and food. For up to three weeks, the adults carry them on their backs into the water. They continue following and begging from their parents until fledging at roughly ten to eleven weeks.
sections.ecology: The grebe is a predator of fish and aquatic invertebrates, and in turn may be prey for larger aquatic hunters. Its floating nest occupies the boundary between open water and emergent plants. Eurasian coots eat grebe eggs; a departing parent covers its clutch with nest material, concealing it from this predator. Reeds conceal nests, while waves, boats and changing water levels can expose or damage eggs.
sections.conservation: BirdLife's global assessment published in 2019 classified the species as Least Concern; southern Africa assessed it separately as Vulnerable in 2025 after a modeled range contraction. Wetland drainage, pollution and disturbance threaten local habitats. In Britain, nineteenth-century demand for grebe skins and feathers in fashionable hats reduced the population to 32 known pairs in England. The Plumage Prohibition was passed in 1921 after bird-protection campaigning. The British population later recovered.
